Antares uses open data from these sources:
The catalogue holds %1$d foods, %2$d% of them with measured vitamins and minerals. Where they are missing, the app says why instead of inventing them.

The authority for Portuguese foods: 1376 foods measured in Portugal, with real Portuguese names. Used with permission from the Instituto Nacional de Saúde Doutor Ricardo Jorge, subject to citation.
Instituto Nacional de Saúde Doutor Ricardo Jorge, I. P. — INSA. Tabela da Composição de Alimentos, v 7.1 [online database]. Lisbon, 2026 [consulted on 29-07-2026]. Available at: https://portfir.insa.min-saude.pt/pt/
The backbone of the catalogue: composition data for over 3000 European foods, published by the French food safety agency under the Etalab 2.0 Open Licence.
Collaborative food product database, under the ODbL licence. Barcode-scanned products come from here and stay on your phone.
Enriches the catalogue with minerals, vitamin E, folate and selenium, and adds foods CIQUAL does not cover. US government public domain.
Dietary Reference Values (DRV) for adults, used in the micronutrient panel.

Why Antares asks for health data

Antares reads your steps, weigh-ins and exercise sessions so you don't have to type them in. That data stays on your phone, in the app's database, and does not leave it — Antares has no server and no account. You can revoke these permissions at any time in Health Connect, and Antares keeps working without them.

This basal rate is about %1$s kcal, give or take %2$s kcal: your body fat came from the tape measure, and the method is off by 3.6 percentage points. Everything below inherits that margin.

Protein: %1$s g per kg of lean mass × %2$s kg = %3$s g. It is higher because you train with weights while in a deficit — Helms et al. (2014) asks for 2.3 to 3.1, rising with how deep the deficit is. With no training logged it would be 1.8.
That is the whole calculation, with no hidden steps. You can check every line by hand: only the multiplication is rounded, and it is rounded to the nearest calorie.
